Gravity is the physical force of attraction between objects, measured by how fast they accelerate towards each other. On Earth, the average gravitational pull is 9.8 meters per second squared (m/s²). This force varies depending on the mass of the objects involved and their distance from each other. Different locations on Earth experience variations in gravitational force due to differences in mass, such as the density of materials like air, rock, and water. 

For example, areas with more mass, like those with a higher density of rock, will have a stronger gravitational pull compared to areas with less mass, such as those with more air. These variations are small, requiring sensitive satellites to measure them accurately.

Gravity is measured by observing how fast objects accelerate towards each other. On Earth, the average gravitational pull is quantified as 9.8 meters per second squared (m/s²). To detect variations in gravitational force around the world, scientists use very sensitive satellites. These satellites can measure tiny differences in gravity, which can be influenced by the density of materials beneath the Earth's surface, such as air, water, and rock.

For instance, regions with a higher density of rock will exhibit a stronger gravitational pull compared to areas with more air. The measurements taken by these satellites are crucial for understanding how gravity varies in different locations due to the differing amounts of mass present.

On Earth, gravity is what keeps us anchored to the surface and varies slightly in different locations due to differences in mass, such as the density of materials like air, rock, and water. This variation in gravitational force is measurable, and scientists use sensitive satellites to detect these differences around the world.
